name: superlocalmemory
description: Local-first persistent memory for coding agents via MCP, with governed recall
readme:
### The governed memory brain for every AI agent. It lives on your machine. It never bluffs. **One memory for every agent you and your team use** — Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Copilot, Antigravity, Hermes, ChatGPT, Claude on the web, Grok Bot, Muse and any harness that speaks MCP or runs a command. Decisions, documents, screenshots and PDFs, recalled the way you ask for them, governed like company data, shared through a mesh where your local agents and web bots talk to each other, and answered honestly: when the answer isn't there, your agent hears *"That isn't in SuperLocalMemory."* — not a confident guess. [![PyPI](https://img.shields.io/pypi/v/superlocalmemory)](https://pypi.org/project/superlocalmemory/) [![npm](https://img.shields.io/npm/v/superlocalmemory)](https://www.npmjs.com/package/superlocalmemory) [![PyPI downloads](https://img.shields.io/pepy/dt/superlocalmemory?label=PyPI%20downloads)](https://pepy.tech/project/superlocalmemory) [![npm downloads](https://img.shields.io/npm/dt/superlocalmemory?label=npm%20downloads)](https://www.npmjs.com/package/superlocalmemory) [![GitHub stars](https://img.shields.io/github/stars/qualixar/superlocalmemory?style=flat&logo=github)](https://github.com/qualixar/superlocalmemory/stargazers) [![License: AGPL-3.0](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-AGPL--3.0-blue)](https://github.com/qualixar/superlocalmemory/blob/main/LICENSE) [![Research: 4 arXiv papers](https://img.shields.io/badge/arXiv-4_papers-b31b1b)](#research) **[Install](#install)** · **[See it work](#30-second-example)** · **[Full demo](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9Y0wAT07KTc)** · **[Every capability](#everything-slm-does)** · **[Docs](#documentation)** · **[Website](https://www.superlocalmemory.com)** **⭐ If SuperLocalMemory keeps your agents from guessing, [star the repo](https://github.com/qualixar/superlocalmemory/stargazers). It helps other developers find it.**
**Agents forget everything between sessions. The usual fix — a vector store with a save button — makes it worse:** it always returns *something*, even when nothing it holds answers the question, and your agent builds on it. This is a memory **brain**, not a bucket: it understands what was saved (who, what, when, which project), keeps it true over time, governs who may see it, and refuses to bluff. Four arXiv papers describe how it works. In Mode A, core remember and recall make no model-provider call: no API key, no cloud account, no Docker. Anything that sends data out is a choice you make, and the docs say exactly what goes. ## Install > **The easiest way: let your AI agent install it.** Copy the block below into Claude Code, Codex, Cursor or any agent that can run commands. It reads the setup guide, asks you one question, sets everything up and tells you what works. No terminal commands for you to learn. ``` Install SuperLocalMemory on this computer for me. Follow https://github.com/qualixar/superlocalmemory/blob/main/SETUP_FOR_AGENTS.md step by step and show me what each step printed. Ask me only one question, before turning on anything optional: whether I also want to find my pictures, screenshots and PDFs by describing them. Connect SuperLocalMemory to the agent I am using. When you finish, run slm doctor and tell me in plain words what works. ``` **No AI agent? One line in Terminal** (macOS and Linux). It brings its own Python, sets everything up, connects the AI tools it finds and opens the dashboard; no Python or npm needed beforehand: ```bash curl -fsSLo get-slm.sh https://raw.githubusercontent.com/qualixar/superlocalmemory/main/scripts/get-slm.sh && sh get-slm.sh ``` Add pictures and documents from the start with `sh get-slm.sh --media` at the end. It downloads the script first, so you can read it before it runs. Windows: use the agent prompt above, or npm or pip below. **Prefer the terminal?** Both routes end in the same setup: your text memory on this machine, and, if you say yes, your pictures and documents too. **npm**, the primary route (Node 18+). It installs SLM into a package-owned virtual environment: ```bash npm install -g superlocalmemory # add --media to also turn on pictures and documents slm setup # pick Mode A to keep everything on this machine slm connect claude-code # or codex, cursor, windsurf, zed, claude-desktop, jetbrains, opencode ... ``` **pip**, the other primary route (Python 3.12 to 3.14), in a Python virtual environment you activate: ```bash python3 -m venv .venv source .venv/bin/activate # Windows: .venv\Scripts\activate python -m pip install superlocalmemory # or, without a venv: pipx install superlocalmemory slm setup slm connect claude-code slm media enable # optional: pictures and documents (about 1.5 GB; needs 16 GB of memory) ``` **uv**: `uv tool install --python 3.12 superlocalmemory` installs `slm` as an isolated tool, with nothing to activate; see [Linux install](https://github.com/qualixar/superlocalmemory/blob/main/docs/install-linux.md#isolated-slm-command-with-uv). **Claude Code plugin:** `claude plugin marketplace add qualixar/superlocalmemory`, then `claude plugin install superlocalmemory@qualixar`. **Codex:** `slm connect codex`, then `slm codex install`. **Two models, one memory.** Text is searched with a small local text model (nomic). If you turn on pictures and documents, a second local model (Google's EmbeddingGemma 2) reads them, and one recall returns both. The picture model unloads after 30 minutes without use, so it holds no memory while you only work with text. Details: [pictures and documents](https://github.com/qualixar/superlocalmemory/blob/main/docs/pictures-and-documents.md), [getting started](https://github.com/qualixar/superlocalmemory/blob/main/docs/getting-started.md), [agent setup steps](https://github.com/qualixar/superlocalmemory/blob/main/SETUP_FOR_AGENTS.md). Repository clone: `./scripts/install.sh install` (macOS, Linux) or `.\scripts\install.ps1 -Action Install` (Windows). Runs on Windows, Linux and Apple Silicon macOS ([platforms](#platform-support)). ## 30-second example ```console $ slm remember "We deploy the API blue-green; rollback is a DNS flip." --kind decision Queryable ✓ 1 facts $ slm remember "Staging DB is Postgres 16 on port 5433." $ slm recall "how do we roll back the API" 1. [0.67] We deploy the API blue-green; rollback is a DNS flip. $ slm recall "zxqv plorth wimble" That isn't in SuperLocalMemory. $ slm remember "Staging DB moved to Postgres 17 on port 5434." --replaces Replaced ✓ 1 fact(s). To undo: slm review-correction ... rollback 1 $ slm recall "which port does staging postgres use" 1. [0.68] Staging DB moved to Postgres 17 on port 5434. ``` Real output from a fresh Mode A install, trimmed. Scores rank memories; they are not probabilities. ## Why SuperLocalMemory: twelve superpowers **1. It knows when it doesn't know.** Every recall comes back in one of three tiers: a **supported** answer; the **closest memories**, labelled *"I don't have this exactly — here are the closest memories"*; or *"That isn't in SuperLocalMemory."* for nonsense. Just after a start it says it is still warming up and shows what it has found, so you never hear "empty" when the truth is "not ready yet". Your agent stops building on the wrong memory. **2. A second opinion that never leaves your Mac.** On Apple Silicon, SLM installs **Laya**, a small on-device model that judges whether the memories found actually answer the question. Prefer the cloud, or not on a Mac? **Jev** does the same check online, only after you tick its consent. **3. Your documents and screenshots become a knowledge base you can ask.** Save a photo, a screenshot or a PDF and find it weeks later by describing it — *"the slide with the quarterly numbers"*. The picture model is **Google's EmbeddingGemma 2**, running on your computer: one model reads both your words and your pictures, so a description finds the image. OCR runs locally too, every PDF page is indexed by its picture and its text, and every answer cites its file and page. No generative model ever looks at your files. **4. Karpathy's LLM-wiki idea, built in — with search kept.** Andrej Karpathy's [LLM-wiki pattern](https://gist.github.com/karpathy/442a6bf555914893e9891c11519de94f) turns raw documents into an organised knowledge base with an index and a health check. SLM does that from the data it already stores — a **document index** of every file with its people, projects and dates, and a **document health check** that finds empty pages, unlinked documents, duplicate pages and contradicted facts — while keeping real hybrid search for the moment you need to *find* something. **5. It looks after itself.** **Memory health** describes your older memories in the background — dates, names, projects, kinds — only ever by adding, never touching what you wrote. Anything that moves or deletes waits for your **Fix**, and **Undo** puts it back. **6. Governed, not just stored.** Every save passes an admission check and gets a receipt. Every read respects roles, workspaces and scopes. Every erasure reaches every copy — summaries, caches, indexes, picture mirrors — and comes with a verifiable receipt. Every action lands in a hash-chained audit trail. Built for teams and for GDPR, not bolted on. **7. Memory with a sense of time.** Every fact knows when it happened and when SLM learned it. Ask what was true last month, or what SLM knew before a date. Corrections replace a fact and stay undoable; unused memories fade the way human memory does. **8. It never floods your context window.** Layered recall gives an agent a one-line glance, the facts, or the full surrounding context — under a hard token budget it sets. The agent digs deeper with `expand` only when it needs to, and cache and reversible compression stop you paying for the same output twice. **9. Many agents, one brain.** Every write records which agent made it, with trust scores against memory poisoning, so ten agents can share one memory without poisoning it. **10. Your agents talk to each other — even across the internet.** Through **SLM-Mesh**, the agents on your computer and the bots on the web finally share one conversation. Claude Code, Codex and Hermes sessions exchange messages, waits, locks and shared state, on one machine or several, so one agent can hand work to another and two never edit the same file at once. And the bots you allow — ChatGPT, Claude on the web, Grok Bot, Muse — join the same mesh: a bot in your browser can message the agent on your laptop by name and read its reply. Every message arrives labelled as data, never as instructions; a web bot reads new messages when its next turn starts. **11. It learns every day, and it can't quietly get worse.** Every reported outcome teaches it: ranking learns which memories actually helped, stable habits become soft prompts for new sessions, and agent skills are measured and revised. A new ranker is promoted only on a statistically valid win and rolled back automatically if it slips. Work runs as **bounded loops** that end only when an independent gate passes — never on an agent's word — and multi-step pipelines run as **bounded graphs** with [Bounded Loops](https://github.com/qualixar/bounded-loops), whose finished runs SLM keeps as read-only evidence. **12. Science, not vibes.** Four arXiv papers back every layer: information-geometric retrieval, biologically inspired forgetting, Bayesian trust against memory poisoning, and governed memory with measured costs. The core math runs without a language model, and the published benchmarks state exactly how they were measured. SuperLocalMemory is part of Qualixar's AI Reliability Engineering work: agent memory that is observable, bounded and honest about what it doesn't know. ## Watch it work
[![Watch the full SuperLocalMemory demo: AI agent memory shared by Claude Code, Codex, ChatGPT and Grok Bot](https://img.youtube.com/vi/9Y0wAT07KTc/maxresdefault.jpg)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9Y0wAT07KTc) *The full eight-minute demo: one memory shared by your coding agents and bots, every tab.*
## Add SuperLocalMemory to your app You do not need to wait for an app store. Every app below can take SuperLocalMemory straight from this GitHub repository, `qualixar/superlocalmemory`, in two steps. **Step 1, once per computer.** Install SuperLocalMemory: `npm install -g superlocalmemory` (or `pipx install superlocalmemory`). **Laya — on your Mac** A small on-device model for Apple Silicon (about 1.1 GB). Installed by default by setup and offered after an upgrade; nothing ever leaves the machine. Opt out with `slm setup --no-laya` or `SLM_SKIP_LAYA=1`. Calibrate it to your own memories in the background with `slm embedder calibrate`. **Jev — online, any computer** The same check on Windows, Linux or macOS, through TypeSafe or OpenRouter with your own key. It sends the question and the top three memories, and only after you tick its consent. It never turns itself on.
The verdict is one input to the support decision, with its own time budget, and the **Answer Check** tab shows verdicts, timing and how often memory had no answer — without storing your questions. Agents forget everything between sessions. The usual fix — a vector store with a save button — makes it worse: it always returns *something*, even when nothing it holds answers the question, and your agent builds on it. This is a memory brain, not a bucket: it understands what was saved (who, what, when, which project), keeps it true over time, governs who may see it, and refuses to bluff. Four arXiv papers describe how it works.

In Mode A, core remember and recall make no model-provider call: no API key, no cloud account, no Docker. Anything that sends data out is a choice you make, and the docs say exactly what goes.

Install

> The easiest way: let your AI agent install it. Copy the block below into Claude Code, Codex, Cursor or any agent that can run commands. It reads the setup guide, asks you one question, sets everything up and tells you what works. No terminal commands for you to learn.


Install SuperLocalMemory on this computer for me. Follow

https://github.com/qualixar/superlocalmemory/blob/main/SETUP_FOR_AGENTS.md

step by step and show me what each step printed. Ask me only one question,

before turning on anything optional: whether I also want to find my pictures,

screenshots and PDFs by describing them. Connect SuperLocalMemory to the agent

I am using. When you finish, run slm doctor and tell me in plain words what works.

No AI agent? One line in Terminal (macOS and Linux). It brings its own Python, sets everything up, connects the AI tools it finds and opens the dashboard; no Python or npm needed beforehand:


curl -fsSLo get-slm.sh https://raw.githubusercontent.com/qualixar/superlocalmemory/main/scripts/get-slm.sh && sh get-slm.sh

Add pictures and documents from the start with sh get-slm.sh --media at the end. It downloads the script first, so you can read it before it runs. Windows: use the agent prompt above, or npm or pip below.

Prefer the terminal? Both routes end in the same setup: your text memory on this machine, and, if you say yes, your pictures and documents too.

npm, the primary route (Node 18+). It installs SLM into a package-owned virtual environment:


npm install -g superlocalmemory   # add --media to also turn on pictures and documents

slm setup                         # pick Mode A to keep everything on this machine

slm connect claude-code           # or codex, cursor, windsurf, zed, claude-desktop, jetbrains, opencode ...

pip, the other primary route (Python 3.12 to 3.14), in a Python virtual environment you activate:


python3 -m venv .venv

source .venv/bin/activate         # Windows: .venv\Scripts\activate

python -m pip install superlocalmemory   # or, without a venv: pipx install superlocalmemory

slm setup

slm connect claude-code

slm media enable                  # optional: pictures and documents (about 1.5 GB; needs 16 GB of memory)

uv: uv tool install --python 3.12 superlocalmemory installs slm as an isolated tool, with nothing to activate; see Linux install.

Claude Code plugin: claude plugin marketplace add qualixar/superlocalmemory, then claude plugin install superlocalmemory@qualixar. Codex: slm connect codex, then slm codex install.

Two models, one memory. Text is searched with a small local text model (nomic). If you turn on pictures and documents, a second local model (Google's EmbeddingGemma 2) reads them, and one recall returns both. The picture model unloads after 30 minutes without use, so it holds no memory while you only work with text. Details: pictures and documents, getting started, agent setup steps.

Repository clone: ./scripts/install.sh install (macOS, Linux) or .\scripts\install.ps1 -Action Install (Windows). Runs on Windows, Linux and Apple Silicon macOS ([platforms](#platform-support)).

$ slm remember "We deploy the API blue-green; rollback is a DNS flip." --kind decision

Queryable ✓ 1 facts

$ slm remember "Staging DB is Postgres 16 on port 5433."

Replaced ✓ 1 fact(s). To undo: slm review-correction ... rollback 1

$ slm recall "which port does staging postgres use"

  1. [0.68] Staging DB moved to Postgres 17 on port 5434.

Why SuperLocalMemory: twelve superpowers

1. It knows when it doesn't know. Every recall comes back in one of three tiers: a supported answer; the closest memories, labelled *"I don't have this exactly — here are the closest memories"*; or *"That isn't in SuperLocalMemory."* for nonsense. Just after a start it says it is still warming up and shows what it has found, so you never hear "empty" when the truth is "not ready yet". Your agent stops building on the wrong memory.

2. A second opinion that never leaves your Mac. On Apple Silicon, SLM installs Laya, a small on-device model that judges whether the memories found actually answer the question. Prefer the cloud, or not on a Mac? Jev does the same check online, only after you tick its consent.

3. Your documents and screenshots become a knowledge base you can ask. Save a photo, a screenshot or a PDF and find it weeks later by describing it — *"the slide with the quarterly numbers"*. The picture model is <img src="https://raw.githubusercontent.com/qualixar/superlocalmemory/main/assets/branding/google-g.svg" width="18" alt="Google"> Google's EmbeddingGemma 2, running on your computer: one model reads both your words and your pictures, so a description finds the image. OCR runs locally too, every PDF page is indexed by its picture and its text, and every answer cites its file and page. No generative model ever looks at your files.

4. Karpathy's LLM-wiki idea, built in — with search kept. Andrej Karpathy's LLM-wiki pattern turns raw documents into an organised knowledge base with an index and a health check. SLM does that from the data it already stores — a document index of every file with its people, projects and dates, and a document health check that finds empty pages, unlinked documents, duplicate pages and contradicted facts — while keeping real hybrid search for the moment you need to *find* something.

5. It looks after itself. Memory health describes your older memories in the background — dates, names, projects, kinds — only ever by adding, never touching what you wrote. Anything that moves or deletes waits for your Fix, and Undo puts it back.

6. Governed, not just stored. Every save passes an admission check and gets a receipt. Every read respects roles, workspaces and scopes. Every erasure reaches every copy — summaries, caches, indexes, picture mirrors — and comes with a verifiable receipt. Every action lands in a hash-chained audit trail. Built for teams and for GDPR, not bolted on.

7. Memory with a sense of time. Every fact knows when it happened and when SLM learned it. Ask what was true last month, or what SLM knew before a date. Corrections replace a fact and stay undoable; unused memories fade the way human memory does.

8. It never floods your context window. Layered recall gives an agent a one-line glance, the facts, or the full surrounding context — under a hard token budget it sets. The agent digs deeper with expand only when it needs to, and cache and reversible compression stop you paying for the same output twice.

9. Many agents, one brain. Every write records which agent made it, with trust scores against memory poisoning, so ten agents can share one memory without poisoning it.

10. Your agents talk to each other — even across the internet. Through SLM-Mesh, the agents on your computer and the bots on the web finally share one conversation. Claude Code, Codex and Hermes sessions exchange messages, waits, locks and shared state, on one machine or several, so one agent can hand work to another and two never edit the same file at once. And the bots you allow — ChatGPT, Claude on the web, Grok Bot, Muse — join the same mesh: a bot in your browser can message the agent on your laptop by name and read its reply. Every message arrives labelled as data, never as instructions; a web bot reads new messages when its next turn starts.

11. It learns every day, and it can't quietly get worse. Every reported outcome teaches it: ranking learns which memories actually helped, stable habits become soft prompts for new sessions, and agent skills are measured and revised. A new ranker is promoted only on a statistically valid win and rolled back automatically if it slips. Work runs as bounded loops that end only when an independent gate passes — never on an agent's word — and multi-step pipelines run as bounded graphs with Bounded Loops, whose finished runs SLM keeps as read-only evidence.

12. Science, not vibes. Four arXiv papers back every layer: information-geometric retrieval, biologically inspired forgetting, Bayesian trust against memory poisoning, and governed memory with measured costs. The core math runs without a language model, and the published benchmarks state exactly how they were measured.

SuperLocalMemory is part of Qualixar's AI Reliability Engineering work: agent memory that is observable, bounded and honest about what it doesn't know.

# SuperLocalMemory

AI agent memory with a local data root. Five candidate producers (semantic, BM25, temporal, spreading-activation, Hopfield) fuse via RRF, with an entity-graph post-fusion score enhancement — all with mathematical similarity scoring. Mode A operates without sending memory content to a cloud model provider; optional connectors, backup, and proxy providers are explicit choices with separate behavior.

## Installation

```bash
pip install superlocalmemory
# or
npm install -g superlocalmemory
```

## Quick Start

```bash
slm remember "Alice works at Google as a Staff Engineer" --json
slm recall "Who is Alice?" --json
slm status --json
```

## Commands

All data-returning commands support `--json` for structured agent-native output.

### Memory Operations

```bash
slm remember "<content>" --json           # Store a memory
slm remember "<content>" --tags "a,b" --json
slm recall "<query>" --json               # Semantic search
slm recall "<query>" --limit 5 --json
slm list --json -n 20                     # List recent memories
slm forget "<query>" --json               # Preview matches (add --yes to delete)
slm forget "<query>" --json --yes         # Delete matching memories
slm delete <fact_id> --json --yes         # Delete specific memory by ID
slm update <fact_id> "<content>" --json   # Update a memory
```

### Pictures, documents and folders (4.1.25, optional)

Off by default. Needs a computer with 16 GB of memory and downloads about 1.5 GB.
Ask the user before turning it on.

```bash
slm media status --json                   # is it on, and how is set-up going
slm media enable                          # asks first; --yes skips the question (only with the user's yes)
slm media disable                         # memories are kept
slm media repair --dry-run                # count pictures that cannot be found by what they show yet
slm sources add ~/Notes --kind obsidian   # or --kind folder; read-only; shows what would be read, then asks
slm sources list --json
```

When it is on, a normal `slm recall` also returns saved pictures and PDF pages (a
`media` block per result). The MCP tools are `remember_media`, `remember_document`,
`get_media`, `media_status` and, for web apps, `media_upload_link`; they are listed
only in the `full`, `power` and `whole` tool sets. A picture is up to 25 MB, a PDF up
to 100 MB and 500 pages. Do not save a file that shows a secret. The `slm-media` skill
has the details.

### Company mode and the dashboard key

```bash
slm team status --json                    # Require login: on|off, user count
slm team policy --require-login on|off    # on the SLM computer; only when the user asks
slm token show                            # the key the dashboard asks for in strict mode; a secret, never paste it into chat
```

### Diagnostics

```bash
slm status --json                         # System status (mode, profile, DB)
slm health --json                         # Math layer health
slm trace "<query>" --json                # Recall with per-channel breakdown
```

### Configuration

```bash
slm mode --json                           # Get current mode
slm mode a --json                         # Set mode (a=local, b=ollama, c=cloud)
slm profile list --json                   # List profiles
slm profile switch <name> --json          # Switch profile
slm profile create <name> --json          # Create profile
slm connect --json                        # Auto-configure IDEs
slm connect --list --json                 # List supported IDEs
```

### Bounded Loops

```bash
slm loop demo                             # Run built-in convergence demo (no API key needed)
slm loop history [--name <loop-name>]     # List recorded runs from SLM memory
slm loop show <run_id>                    # Show every lap of one run
```

Loop laps are persisted to SLM memory under the tag `loop:<name>`. MCP tools
`slm_loop_run`, `slm_loop_history`, and `slm_loop_show` are available in the
`code` and `full` profiles.

```bash
slm mcp                                   # Start MCP server (for IDE integration)
slm dashboard                             # Open web dashboard
slm warmup                                # Pre-download embedding model
```

## JSON Envelope

Every `--json` response follows a consistent envelope:

```json
{
  "success": true,
  "command": "recall",
  "version": "4.0.0",
  "data": {
    "results": [
      {"fact_id": "abc123", "score": 0.87, "content": "Alice works at Google"}
    ],
    "count": 1,
    "query_type": "semantic"
  },
  "next_actions": [
    {"command": "slm list --json", "description": "List recent memories"}
  ]
}
```

Error responses:

```json
{
  "success": false,
  "command": "recall",
  "version": "4.0.0",
  "error": {"code": "ENGINE_ERROR", "message": "Description of what went wrong"}
}
```

## Operating Modes

| Mode | Description | Cloud Required |
|------|-------------|----------------|
| A | Local Guardian -- core memory runs without a cloud model provider; optional connectors and model downloads may use the network | None (for core memory) |
| B | Smart Local -- a model on this machine (Ollama by default, any local server works), data stays on your machine | Local only |
| C | Full Power -- your own endpoint, or a cloud provider, for maximum accuracy | Yes, unless using a keyless custom endpoint |

SuperLocalMemory works via both MCP and CLI:
